description: We build tools that use NASA satellite radar and Earth data to understand how the ground moves, especially in cities built on clay. SWELL explores the difference between real ground movement and changes caused by wet soil, helping communities see what is happening beneath their feet and make better decisions about their infrastructure.
summary: SWELL is an interactive digital twin that uses NASA Earth observation data to investigate ground movement in cities built on clay. Starting with Dallas–Fort Worth, Texas, SWELL combines NISAR satellite radar observations with rainfall, soil, land-cover and ground-reference data to investigate the difference between real ground movement and radar changes caused by wet soil. Users can explore ground conditions, test scenarios involving drainage, paving and green space, and compare modeled outcomes through interactive maps and 3D visualizations. SWELL aims to turn complex satellite observations into understandable, evidence-based information for city planners, water utilities, engineers and emergency managers, while making uncertainty and scientific limitations visible.

SWELL — A NISAR DIGITAL TWIN FOR CITIES ON CLAY

OVERVIEW

SWELL is an interactive Earth-observation and decision-support platform designed to investigate ground movement in clay-rich urban environments. Starting with Dallas–Fort Worth, Texas, SWELL brings together NASA satellite radar observations, environmental datasets, soil properties, ground-reference measurements and physical modeling in one interactive workspace.

The central question behind SWELL is simple: when satellite radar detects a change in the ground, did the ground actually move, or did changing soil moisture affect the radar signal?

This distinction matters because expansive clay soils naturally shrink and swell as their moisture content changes. These movements can affect roads, foundations, pipes and other infrastructure. At the same time, wet soil can change radar backscatter and interfere with the interpretation of satellite observations.

SWELL aims to investigate these effects separately, communicate uncertainty and help users explore what different environmental and infrastructure decisions could mean.

  1. NASA EARTH OBSERVATION AND DATA INTEGRATION

SWELL uses NASA–ISRO NISAR data, including GUNW and GCOV products, as its central radar observation sources.

The application brings radar observations together with:

  • NASA POWER rainfall and weather information.
  • NASA GIBS and Earthdata resources.
  • USGS elevation and reference information.
  • ESA WorldCover land-cover data.
  • SoilGrids soil-property information.
  • Nevada Geodetic Laboratory GPS reference observations.

These datasets provide different perspectives on the same landscape. Radar observations describe changes in the radar measurement, rainfall provides environmental context, soil properties help characterize clay-rich areas, land-cover information identifies paved and vegetated surfaces, and GPS provides an independent ground-motion reference.

The objective is to make these sources useful together rather than treating any single dataset as a complete explanation of ground movement.

  1. RADAR INTERPRETATION AND GROUND-MOVEMENT ANALYSIS

A major part of SWELL is its attempt to distinguish actual ground movement from misleading radar changes.

The processing workflow includes NISAR interferometric observations, ionospheric and tropospheric correction layers, coherence screening and analysis of wet-soil effects.

SWELL represents the radar change as separate components:

  • Observed radar line-of-sight (LOS) change.
  • A possible contribution from wet-soil effects.
  • An estimated ground-movement component.

The interface allows users to inspect individual radar cells, observation dates, coherence values and candidate measurements. Low-quality or unreliable observations can be withheld rather than presented as certain measurements.

For example, users can inspect a selected LOS change alongside its coherence value and observation period. The interface also identifies where radar evidence is insufficient to support a confident interpretation.

This is important because radar line-of-sight displacement is not automatically equivalent to vertical ground movement, structural damage or flood risk.

  1. INDEPENDENT GROUND-REFERENCE EVIDENCE

SWELL includes a GPS/GNSS evidence workflow to compare satellite-derived observations with independent ground-reference information.

Users can retrieve available ground stations and inspect their observation coverage, including the number of available dates for individual stations.

The intention is to provide an additional reference when evaluating satellite-derived changes rather than relying exclusively on the radar measurements.

The application also makes the limitations of these comparisons visible. GPS observations do not automatically validate every radar cell or establish the cause of a particular change.

  1. CLAY PHYSICS AND PREDICTIVE MODELING

SWELL combines clay-response physics with a physics-informed network to investigate how soil and ground conditions respond to changing environmental inputs.

The modeling workflow includes:

  • Clay-related soil response.
  • Rainfall and moisture inputs.
  • Land-cover and paving conditions.
  • Ground movement and modeled displacement.
  • A Kalman-filter-based state-estimation workflow.
  • A physics-informed network evaluated against alternative models.

The digital twin operates across approximately 3,600 model cells and includes uncertainty information with its forecasts.

The physics-informed network is evaluated against a no-change baseline, the same network without its physics component, and a plain physical equation.

This comparison is important because a complicated model should demonstrate value beyond simply assuming that conditions remain unchanged.

  1. INTERACTIVE EARTH WORKSPACE AND DIGITAL TWIN

The Earth Workspace is one of the main interactive parts of SWELL.

Instead of only displaying a static satellite map, users can directly interact with the modeled landscape and investigate how changing environmental or infrastructure conditions affect the simulation.

Users can:

  • Paint changes in water, drainage, paving and green-space conditions.
  • Define rainfall scenarios by entering storm inputs.
  • Change rainfall intensity and baseline infiltration assumptions.
  • Adjust Manning roughness.
  • Define a proposed intervention footprint.
  • Compare baseline and intervention scenarios under the same storm.
  • Inspect before-and-after results.
  • View corresponding map, 3D terrain and chart outputs.

The map, three-dimensional representation and charts are driven by the same underlying scenario inputs and model equations.

The application also provides contextual information about the selected area, including modeled footprint size, contributing area and intervention assumptions.

The 3D city workspace uses terrain and city visualization, including buildings and photorealistic Dallas representations.

This allows users to explore not just where a change occurs, but how different scenarios affect the modeled environment.

  1. INTERVENTION COMPARISON AND WATER-BALANCE ANALYSIS

SWELL includes a comparison workflow for testing alternative interventions.

Users can run the same storm conditions against different scenarios, compare modeled water storage and inspect the resulting differences.

The interface includes:

  • Baseline and intervention comparisons.
  • Rainfall-volume inputs.
  • Modeled peak water depth.
  • Intervention capture volume.
  • Stored-water differences.
  • Sensitivity testing.
  • Alternative infiltration assumptions.
  • Changes in model assumptions and their consequences.

The sensitivity workflow compares alternative cases, including different time steps and infiltration assumptions.

The application also makes clear when a result is conditional on idealized assumptions. For example, an idealized sink or closed model boundary should not be interpreted as a verified drainage installation or real-world pipe design.

These distinctions are important because a modeled improvement is not automatically proof that a proposed infrastructure project will work in the real world.

  1. DECISION SUPPORT FOR DIFFERENT USERS

SWELL is designed to translate the same underlying digital twin into information relevant to different people who make decisions about infrastructure and land.

The application supports seven intended user perspectives:

CITY PLANNERS:
Compare paving, drainage and other land-use scenarios under the same rainfall conditions. Examine modeled surface-water and ground-response differences before considering a planning decision.

WATER UTILITIES:
Investigate locations where additional water may influence modeled ground conditions. Generate inspection-oriented information that can be compared with available pipe and infrastructure records.

EMERGENCY MANAGERS:
Explore heavy-rainfall scenarios, identify areas with higher modeled responses and prioritize locations for further inspection.

ENGINEERS:
Review measured seasonal movement, uncertainty and modeled conditions to identify areas that may require closer engineering investigation.

RESIDENTS:
Receive accessible explanations of modeled local conditions, including seasonal movement estimates and land-cover context. The information is intended to support awareness, not replace professional structural assessments.

INSURERS:
Explore location-based evidence and modeled environmental conditions that may be relevant to further risk investigation.

RESEARCHERS:
Inspect the underlying observations, assumptions, model comparisons and evidence used to produce the results.

The goal is to provide different users with relevant information without changing the underlying scientific evidence.

  1. DECISION PACKAGES AND EVIDENCE EXPORT

SWELL includes a decision-package workflow that converts a modeled scenario into supporting files.

The application can export a ZIP package containing:

  • CSV files.
  • GeoJSON files.
  • Scenario JSON.
  • Supporting evidence.
  • A decision log.

These outputs allow users to take information from the interactive application into other tools and review workflows.

The decision workflow also identifies the need for a named human decision-maker. SWELL does not automatically approve infrastructure projects or replace professional engineering responsibility.

  1. VERIFICATION, TESTING AND SCIENTIFIC TRANSPARENCY

SWELL includes a dedicated verification workflow rather than presenting its predictions as automatically correct.

Its evaluation includes seven tests defined in advance and approximately 110 automated software tests.

The presentation documents testing on eight NISAR observation pairs covering July 5 to October 21, 2026.

The evaluation compares held-out NISAR observations against a no-change baseline and alternative model configurations.

Some findings are encouraging. For example, the project reports a correlation of 0.64 between its wetness index and NASA soil-wetness information over 136 days.

However, the project also reports important limitations. Its current forecasts do not yet outperform the no-change baseline, and approximately 17 mm of atmospheric noise was identified in the eight provisional observation pairs.

SWELL makes these limitations visible instead of presenting preliminary results as established scientific accuracy.

The verification interface brings together radar observations, atmospheric correction layers, GPS references and other evidence so that users can inspect what supports a result and what remains uncertain.

  1. CONNECTIONS AND DATA PROVENANCE

SWELL includes a Connections workflow that links the NASA data archive to the processing and modeling application.

The project provides a build and processing record so that users can inspect how data moves through the system.

Scientific provenance and audit information are intended to help users understand the origin of observations, the processing applied to them and the assumptions used in the final outputs.

The project aims to make its analytical workflow more reproducible and transparent.

  1. CONTEXTUAL AI ASSISTANCE

SWELL includes an optional contextual AI explanation feature.

Users can ask questions about a particular run and receive a natural-language explanation of the comparison, assumptions, limitations and suggested next steps.

The AI component is an explanatory interface only. Numerical results are produced by the saved scientific modeling workflow, not generated by the language model.

The application explicitly distinguishes AI-generated explanations from scientific measurements and independent validation.

  1. TECHNOLOGY, IMPLEMENTATION AND FUTURE DEVELOPMENT

SWELL combines Python-based scientific processing, geospatial datasets, radar analysis, physical modeling, a physics-informed network, interactive browser-based visualizations and an evidence-export workflow.

Its architecture brings data processing, model execution, visualization, verification and decision support together in one application.

The initial focus is Dallas–Fort Worth, but the longer-term objective is to make the approach applicable to other cities with expansive clay soils.

Future development includes:

  • Validation across a complete wet–dry season.
  • Combining ascending and descending NISAR observations to investigate vertical and horizontal movement.
  • Additional GPS and Sentinel-1 reference comparisons.
  • Further atmospheric correction and radar-brightness analysis.
  • Expanding the workflow to other cities and geographic regions.

The same general Earth-observation approach may also inspire future investigations of changing surfaces on other planetary bodies, including Mars, the Moon, Venus, Europa and Titan. These are future research possibilities, not currently validated SWELL capabilities.

CONCLUSION

SWELL brings satellite radar, environmental information, soil-response modeling, interactive scenario testing and evidence-based decision support into one workspace.

Its purpose is not simply to show where the ground may be changing. It is to investigate why the observations change, explore how environmental and infrastructure conditions may contribute, show where uncertainty remains and help people decide what should be investigated next.

By connecting NASA Earth observation data to practical questions about roads, buildings, water systems and urban resilience, SWELL aims to make complex scientific information more accessible, transparent and useful to the communities that depend on it.
